title: How To Speak So Students Listen
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies how a teacher speaks — not just what they say — as a decisive factor in classroom listening. He offers three specific changes: talking less overall so that words carry more weight, lowering one's voice so students must lean in and pay closer attention, and giving directions only once to build urgency and personal responsibility. He warns that these strategies may initially backfire, since students accustomed to a teacher shouldering the burden of getting their attention may test the new approach by ignoring it at first. This temporary regression, he explains, reveals how deeply learned helplessness has taken hold, and teachers should stay the course rather than reverting to old habits. Over time, students begin tracking the teacher's movements, anticipating directions, and taking pride in completing tasks independently — outcomes Linsin frames as evidence that responsibility has shifted appropriately from teacher to student.
points: Teachers who talk less give their words greater impact and make them easier for students to tune into.
Lowering your voice, rather than raising it, causes students to instinctively lean in and pay closer attention.
Repeating directions trains students not to listen the first time; saying it once creates urgency.
These strategies may temporarily worsen behavior as students test a newly shifted balance of responsibility.
Over time, students who take ownership of listening become more engaged, attentive, and self-directed.
quotes: If you cut the amount of talking you do by a third, and focus only on what your students need to know, then what you say will have greater impact.
When you lower your voice, however, and speak just loud enough for students in the back of the room to hear, they instinctively lean in. They stop moving and rustling.
When you repeat the same directions over and over, you train your students not to listen to you the first time. You encourage apathy and lighten their load of responsibility.
Because your students have grown accustomed to you taking on the burden for their listening, they may very well ignore you.
They’ll begin looking at you, tracking your movements, and anticipating what you want them to do next.
They’ll become empowered to do for themselves because responsibility feels good. It’s important. It fills with pride.
